concepts.title: sequence representation
concepts.one_liner: Sequences are represented as functions $\ell (x,y,t)$ of spatial coordinates and time, typically discretized as $\ell [n,m,t]$ for processing.
concepts.content: Sequences are represented as functions $\ell (x,y,t)$, where $x,y$ are the spatial coordinates and $t$ is time. When processing sequences, we work with the discretized version represented as $\ell [n,m,t]$, where $n,m$ are the pixel indices and $t$ is the frame number. Discrete sequences are bounded in space and time and can be stored as arrays of size $N \times M \times P$.
concepts.motivation_md: To process video or time-varying visual data, we need a mathematical framework that extends 2D image representations into a third dimension representing time.
concepts.recap_md: - Continuous sequences are functions of space $(x,y)$ and time $t$.

concepts.title: globally moving image model
concepts.one_liner: A globally moving image model describes a sequence where an initial image translates with a constant velocity $(v_x, v_y)$ over time.
concepts.content:
A special sequence occurs when the image has a global motion with constant velocity $(v_x,v_y)$. In such a case, we can write:
$$
\ell (x,y,t) = \ell _0 (x-v_xt,y-v_yt)
$$
where $\ell _0(x,y)= \ell (x,y,0)$ is the image being translated, and $v_x$ and $v_y$ are constants. At time $t$, the image $\ell _0(x,y)$ is translated by the vector $(v_x t, v_y t)$. Consequently, the pixel value at location $(x=0, y=0)$ at time $t=0$ will appear at time $T$ in location $(x=v_x T, y=v_y T)$.
concepts.motivation_md: This model provides a simple mathematical way to describe uniform motion across an entire frame, serving as a building block for more complex motion estimation.
concepts.recap_md: - Global motion is modeled by translating the initial image $\ell_0$ by $(v_x t, v_y t)$.

concepts.title: constant brightness assumption
concepts.one_liner: The constant brightness assumption hypothesizes that the brightness of pixels remains unchanged as they move through a scene.
concepts.content: The constant brightness assumption assumes that the brightness of the pixels does not change while the scene is moving. Using continuous values for $x$, $y$, and $t$, along with continuous images $\ell _0(x,y)$, allows for the handling of any velocity values under this assumption. This hypothesis serves as the initial basis for most motion estimation algorithms.
concepts.motivation_md: Without assuming that an object's appearance stays relatively constant as it moves, it would be mathematically difficult to track pixels from one frame to the next.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes pixel intensity is invariant to motion.

concepts.title: moving object over static background model
concepts.one_liner: This model represents a sequence as a moving object with a binary mask occluding a static background.
concepts.content:
A sequence containing a moving object over a static background can be modeled as:
$$
\ell (x,y,t) = b(x,y) (1-m(x-v_xt,y-v_yt)) + o(x-v_xt,y-v_yt) m(x-v_x t,y-v_y t)
$$
where $b(x,y)$ is the static background image, $o(x,y)$ is the object image moving with speed $(v_x,v_y)$, and $m(x,y)$ is a binary mask that moves with the object. This mask models the fact that the object occludes the background as it moves.
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world video often involves specific objects moving independently of their surroundings; this model mathematically separates the foreground motion from the static environment.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines a static background $b(x,y)$ and a moving object $o(x,y)$.

$$

concepts.title: Fourier transform of a globally moving image

position.section_title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

concepts.one_liner: The Fourier transform of a globally moving image relates spatial frequencies to temporal frequency via a Dirac delta function.
concepts.content:
The Fourier transform (FT) of a globally moving image is derived using the shift property:
$$
\mathscr{L} (w_x,w_y,w_t) = \mathscr{L}_0 (w_x, w_y) \delta (w_t + v_x w_x + v_y w_y)
$$
concepts.motivation_md: Analyzing motion in the frequency domain reveals that the energy of a moving image lies on a specific plane, which is useful for velocity estimation and filter design.
concepts.recap_md: - The FT of a moving image is constrained by a delta function $\delta (w_t + v_x w_x + v_y w_y)$.

concepts.title: sinc function

position.section_title: Modeling sequences in the Fourier domain

concepts.one_liner: The sinc function is the Fourier transform of a box kernel, characterized by a central maximum and decreasing oscillations.
concepts.content:
The sinc function is the Fourier transform of a box kernel. In the continuous domain, the sinc function has the form:
$$
\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin (\pi x)}{\pi x}
$$
This function has its maximum at $x=0$ and then has decreasing oscillations.

concepts.title: causal filters
concepts.one_liner: Causal filters are systems where the output at any time depends only on current and past values of the input.
concepts.content: Causal filters are filters with output variations that only depend on the past values of the input. This requirement imposes the constraint that $h [n,m,t]=0$ for all $t<0$. This means that if the input is an impulse at $t=0$, the output will only have non-zero values for $t>0$. If this condition is satisfied, the filter output will only depend on the input's past for all possible inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: In real-time systems, we cannot use information from the future; causality ensures a filter can be implemented in a physical, time-forward system.
concepts.recap_md: - Output depends only on past and present inputs.

concepts.title: nulling filter
concepts.one_liner: A nulling filter is a spatiotemporal filter designed to cancel objects moving at a specific velocity by computing derivatives along specific space-time orientations.
concepts.content:
A nulling filter $h(x,y,t;v_x,v_y)$ is a kernel used as a spatiotemporal filter to cancel objects moving at a specific velocity $(v_x,v_y)$. It is defined by computing the gradient of the Gaussian along the vector $[1,v_x,v_y]$:

$$h(x,y,t;v_x,v_y) = g_t+v_xg_x+v_yg_y = \nabla  g \left( 1,v_x,v_y \right)^\top$$

When this filter is convolved with an input sequence $\text{img}_0 (x-v_x t,y-v_y t)$, the output is zero due to the brightness constancy constraint:

$$\begin{split}\ell _0 (x-v_x t, y-v_y t) \circ h & = \ell _0 (x-v_x t, y-v_y t) \circ \left( g_t + v_x g_x + v_y g_y \right) \\& = \left( \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial t} + v_x \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial x} + v_y \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial y} \right) \circ g \\& = 0\end{split}$$

By using different filters, each computing derivatives along different space-time orientations, specific objects can be made to disappear from output sequences. As this filter is 3D, it can be visualized as a sequence for different velocities, where each row corresponds to a particular velocity $(v_x, v_y)$. For example, a Gaussian with width $\sigma^2=\sigma_t^2=1.5$ discretized as a $7 \times 7 \times 7$ array can be used to generate filters for velocities such as $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, and $(-1,0)$.
concepts.motivation_md: In video processing, we often want to isolate or remove objects based on their motion. The nulling filter solves this by creating a mathematical 'blind spot' for a specific velocity, allowing us to selectively cancel out parts of a scene that match that motion profile.
concepts.recap_md: - A nulling filter is constructed from the spatiotemporal gradient of a Gaussian kernel.

concepts.title: anti-causal filters
concepts.one_liner: Anti-causal filters are systems where the output depends only on future values of the input.
concepts.content: Anti-causal filters are the opposite of causal filters; in these systems, the output depends only on the future. Mathematically, this is expressed as $h [n,m,t ]=0$ for all $t>0$.
concepts.motivation_md: While physical real-time systems must be causal, anti-causal filters are useful in offline signal processing where the entire dataset is available, allowing for symmetric operations that don't introduce phase lag.
concepts.recap_md: - Output depends exclusively on future input values.

concepts.title: Heaviside step function
concepts.one_liner: The Heaviside step function $u[t]$ is a fundamental signal that is zero for negative time and one otherwise.
concepts.content:
The Heaviside step function, $u[t]$, is an infinite length function defined as:
$$
u [t ] = \begin{cases}
    0     & \quad \text{if }  t <0 \\
    1     & \quad \text{otherwise }\\
\end{cases}$$

concepts.title: IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters
concepts.one_liner: IIR filters are systems whose impulse response has infinite support, often characterized by their stability or instability.
concepts.content: Most filters described by difference equations have an impulse response with infinite support and are called IIR (Infinite Impulse Response) filters. IIR filters can be further classified as stable and unstable. Stable filters are those that, given a bounded input $| \ell _{in} [n,m,t ] |<A$, produce a bounded output $| \ell _{out} [n,m,t ] | <B$. For this to occur, the impulse response must be bounded. In unstable filters, the amplitude of the impulse response diverges to infinity. For example, a filter may be stable if and only if $| \alpha | < 1$.
concepts.motivation_md: IIR filters are often more computationally efficient than FIR filters because they can achieve a desired frequency response using fewer coefficients through recursion.
concepts.recap_md: - Characterized by an impulse response with infinite support.

concepts.title: spatiotemporal Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: The spatiotemporal Gaussian is a low-pass filter that extends the spatial Gaussian into the time domain.
concepts.content:
As with the spatial case, we can define low-pass filters such as the box filter or triangular filters in space and time. The spatiotemporal Gaussian is a trivial extension of the spatial Gaussian filter:
$$g(x,y,t; \sigma_x,\sigma_t) = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^{3/2} \sigma_x^2\sigma_t} \exp{-\frac{x^2 + y^2}{2 \sigma_x^2}} \exp{-\frac{t^2}{2 \sigma_t^2}}$$
concepts.motivation_md: It allows for simultaneous smoothing of spatial features and temporal noise in video data, providing a principled way to handle 3D image volumes.
concepts.recap_md: - Extends the 2D spatial Gaussian to a 3D (x, y, t) volume.

concepts.title: skewed Gaussian filter
concepts.one_liner: A skewed Gaussian filter isolates objects moving at a specific velocity while blurring the rest of the sequence.
concepts.content:
A filter that keeps sharp objects moving at a specific velocity $(v_x,v_y)$ while blurring the rest can be obtained by skewing the Gaussian:
$$g_{v_x,v_y}(x,y,t) = g(x - v_xt,y - v_yt, t)$$
This directional blur is not a rotation of the original Gaussian as the change of variables is not unitary, but the same effect could be obtained with a rotation. For instance, when $v_x=-1, v_y=0$, the sequence is blurred everywhere except for one oriented band corresponding to the motion. When $v_x=1, v_y=0$, the output looks as if the camera was tracking one of the objects while the shutter was open, producing a blurry image of all other objects.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique is used to selectively enhance or track objects moving at a known velocity within a video while suppressing background noise and other moving elements.
concepts.recap_md: - Created by shifting Gaussian spatial coordinates relative to time.

concepts.title: temporal derivatives
concepts.one_liner: Temporal derivatives are used to locate moving objects by measuring changes in signal intensity over time.
concepts.content:
Spatial derivatives are useful for finding regions of image variation such as object boundaries. Similarly, temporal derivatives can be used to locate moving objects. For discrete signals, we can approximate a temporal derivative as:
$$\ell [m,n,t] - \ell [m,n,t-1]$$
concepts.motivation_md: Detecting motion requires identifying where and how much a signal changes between frames; the temporal derivative is the simplest mathematical operator for this task.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the rate of change of intensity at a fixed pixel over time.

concepts.title: spatiotemporal gradient of a Gaussian
concepts.one_liner: The spatiotemporal gradient of a Gaussian combines spatial and temporal derivatives to analyze changes in smoothed video data.
concepts.content:
It is useful to compute temporal derivatives of spatiotemporal Gaussians:
$$\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} = \frac{-t}{\sigma_t^2} g(x,y,t)$$
where $g(x,y,t)$ is the spatiotemporal Gaussian. We can compute the full spatiotemporal gradient as:
$$\nabla  g = \left( g_x(x,y,t), g_y(x,y,t), g_t(x,y,t) \right) =  \left(-x/\sigma^2, -y/\sigma^2, -t/\sigma_t^2 \right) g(x,y,t)$$
concepts.motivation_md: Computing derivatives on a Gaussian-smoothed signal provides a robust way to estimate gradients that is resistant to high-frequency noise in video sequences.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines spatial and temporal derivatives into a single vector.

slots.motivation: Computing derivatives on a Gaussian-smoothed signal provides a robust way to estimate gradients that is resistant to high-frequency noise in video sequences.
slots.key_passage: - Combines spatial and temporal derivatives into a single vector.
slots.example:

$$\frac{\partial g}{\partial t} = \frac{-t}{\sigma_t^2} g(x,y,t)$$
where $g(x,y,t)$ is the spatiotemporal Gaussian. We can compute the full spatiotemporal gradient as:
$$\nabla  g = \left( g_x(x,y,t), g_y(x,y,t), g_t(x,y,t) \right) =  \left(-x/\sigma^2, -y/\sigma^2, -t/\sigma_t^2 \right) g(x,y,t)$$

concepts.title: brightness constancy derivative relation
concepts.one_liner: The brightness constancy derivative relation links temporal and spatial derivatives to describe the motion of an image.
concepts.content:
In the case of a moving image with velocity $(v_x, v_y)$, the sequence is defined as $\ell (x,y,t) = \ell _0 (x-v_xt,y-v_yt)$. We can compute the temporal derivative of $\ell(x,y,t)$ as:
$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial t} = -v_x \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial x} - v_y \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial y}$$
This result shows that for a moving image, there is a relationship between the temporal derivative of the sequence and the spatial derivatives along the direction of motion. This relationship can be used to find a linear combination of temporal and spatial derivatives such that the output is zero.
concepts.motivation_md: This relation is the mathematical foundation for optical flow algorithms, allowing the estimation of object velocity from observed changes in image intensity.
concepts.recap_md: - Relates temporal change to spatial gradients and velocity.

slots.motivation: This relation is the mathematical foundation for optical flow algorithms, allowing the estimation of object velocity from observed changes in image intensity.
slots.key_passage: - Relates temporal change to spatial gradients and velocity.
slots.example:

$$\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial t} = -v_x \frac{\partial \ell _0}{\partial x} - v_y \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial y}$$
This result shows that for a moving image, there is a relationship between the temporal derivative of the sequence and the spatial derivatives along the direction of motion. This relationship can be used to find a linear combination of temporal and spatial derivatives such that the output is zero.
